newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Weeds said no threat to Saudi wheat, barley crop.
newsitem.headline: Weeds said no threat to Saudi wheat, barley crop.

text.p: Some Saudi wheat and barley crops have been affected by weeds which have become resistant to a herbicide continuously used by some farmers, a Saudi-based grain specialist said.
But he told Reuters in an interview the weed problem would not have a serious impact on the kingdom's wheat or barley output.

"Wheat and barley have been affected on some fields," he said. "For the last 12 years, some people have grown crops continuously in the same field, using the same herbicide year after year. So these weeds have become resistant."
Local newspapers have reported concern among farmers that output could be threatened by the herbicide-resistant weeds.

The grains expert said the problem, which has existed for years, could be magnified this year, but he nevertheless said output would not be seriously affected. He said some farmers who mistakenly thought they had successfully cleaned their fields, had replanted wheat and barley and the weeds had reappeared.
"The farmers who made a muddle with the weeds are the same ones who have low production. It won't affect the good ones who have higher output," he said.

"I still forecast wheat production of 1.5-1.8 million tonnes this year or more," the grain expert said, referring to the September 1996 to August 1997 season. This was up from an estimated 1.2 million tonnes the previous year.
He did not have a figure for estimated barley production, which other farm analysts put at 450,000 tonnes last year.
Local wheat consumption is about 1.8 million tonnes.
The expert said the herbicide used, known as Hograss or Hoelon, was marketed by Germany's Hoechst AG.
Saudi Arabia is the world's single largest barley buyer. Analysts expect imports of about six million tonnes in 1997.
